title: That they all may be one (John 17:20–23)
hookLine: his prayer for unity, the charter of Christian unity work
last: YOUR JOY NO MAN SHALL TAKE.

lines: THE LAST THING HE DOES: PRAY.
cards: On a single street in many towns you can find a Catholic parish, a Baptist church, a Greek Orthodox church and a Lutheran one, each with its own sign out front. Every Sunday they read from the same Gospels.

Christians have been divided for a long time, some splits many centuries old, some newer. So it's striking that, in John's Gospel, the last thing Jesus does before he walks out to the garden is pray out loud.
And part of what he prays for is the people on that street.

teach.b: John seventeen is sometimes called the high priestly prayer. Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays for himself, then for the disciples at the table.
Then he looks further: not for them only, but for those who will believe in me through their word. That's everyone after them.

teach.h: ONE AS THE FATHER AND SON.
teach.b: And here's what he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice the measure.
Not one the way a club or a company is one. One as the Father and the Son are one. And notice the reason: that the world may believe.
Unity isn't a private comfort. It's a sign, the same way the new commandment was a sign. Catholics call efforts toward Christian unity ecumenism, and they point to this prayer as its charter.
In 1964 the Second Vatican Council issued a decree on ecumenism, saying that division openly contradicts the will of Christ.
In 1995 Pope John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on Christian unity and gave it this prayer's Latin as its title: Ut unum sint, that they may be one.
Each January, in many places, Catholics, Orthodox and Protestant Christians keep a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity together.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: That's week seventy-five: eirene, the vine, greater love, friends, truth, joy, and now, that they may be one.

how: Each January, Catholics in many places join Orthodox and Protestant Christians in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and the Mass includes prayers for the unity of Christians.

games.q: it's your last evening with your friends. you pray out loud for the people who will believe because of them, centuries later. what do you ask for?
o: that they all may be one.
that they'll be safe from harm.
games.why: that they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee, that the world may believe.

practice: Picture the churches near you, all of them, not just your own, the buildings and the people inside, and someone you love who worships somewhere different, or who stopped going.
Don't argue anything in your head; just hold them side by side. If you pray, pray Jesus's own words for them, that they all may be one; if you don't, simply picture them gathered in one place.

wordCard.voice: Ecumenism. Catholics' word for the work toward Christian unity, rooted in Jesus's prayer the night before he died, that all who would believe might be one, a sign to the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: that they all may be one (John 17:21). Latin: ut omnes unum sint.
